title: Adjective Endings: -ous, -ive, -ible and -ic
short: Endings like -ous (full of), -ive (tending to), -ible and -able (able to be) and -ic (having to do with) make adjectives.
trouble: The ending tells the part of speech, not the meaning: copious, pernicious and impetuous are all adjectives but mean very different things.

blocks.html: A suffix at the end of a word often tells you what kind of word it is. These four endings make adjectives, words that describe: famous, active, readable, heroic.

blocks.html: -ous (also -ious, -uous) = full of, having. -ive = tending to, doing. -ible, -able = able to be, worth being. -ic, -ical = having to do with, like.

The ending tells you the word’s job; the root tells you its meaning. Put them together: timorous is timor (fear) + -ous (full of), full of fear. malleable is malle (hammer) + -able: able to be hammered into shape. cryptic is crypt (hidden) + -ic: having to do with hidden things.

head: Word and meaning
Parts, and what they say
rows:
cred believe + -ible able to be
→ “able to be believed”

malle hammer + -able able to be
→ “able to be hammered (into shape)”

e- out + vas go + -ive tending to
→ “tending to slip out”

crypt hidden + -ic having to do with
→ “having to do with hidden things”

chronic
lasting a long time or coming back again and again

chron time + -ic having to do with
→ “having to do with (long) time”

blocks.title: Let the ending do the work
blocks.q: Fill the blank with the right form: “The witness gave a ______ account of the accident.” Choices: credit, credence, credible, credibly.
steps: The blank comes between a and the noun account, so it needs an adjective.
credit and credence are nouns; credibly is an adverb.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: easily shaped or bent; also, easily influenced
entry.ex: Warm wax is {malleable}, so the children pressed it into star shapes.
entry.ctx: Young children’s tastes are {malleable}; a toddler who hates peas this month may ask for seconds next month after seeing an older cousin enjoy them.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin malleabilis, from malleare (to hammer), from malleus (hammer).

mn.text: A few taps of the smith’s mallet and the soft gold bends into a ring: gold is {malleable}.

blocks.html: Expecting the ending to tell you the meaning. It tells you the part of speech, not what the word means: copious (plentiful), pernicious (harmful) and impetuous (rash) are all adjectives in -ous, but they mean very different things. Use the root for the meaning.
